newsitem.title: ITALY: Judge probes human error in Antonov plane crash.
newsitem.headline: Judge probes human error in Antonov plane crash.

text.p: Human error may have played a part in the crash of an giant Antonov cargo plane which ploughed into a farmhouse while trying to land at Turin airport killing four people, an Italian magistrate said on Wednesday.
"There is certainly a human element," Turin prosecutor Bruno Tinti, who is involved in efforts to identify the cause of Tuesday's crash, told reporters.
He said investigators had not ruled out other causes and would examine the flight recorder which had now been found.

The Russian pilot and co-pilot were killed when the Antonov 124, one of the world's largest aircraft, sliced into buildings in the village of San Francesco al Campo as it came in to land on a flight from Moscow with 23 people on board.
Two villagers also died when they were buried in rubble.

The body of a 55-year-old man was found under a dead cow on Tuesday near a shattered farm building where rescue workers were still trying on Wednesday to recover the corpse of the dead man's 59-year-old wife.

Hospital sources said 13 crew members had been treated for injuries while another eight escaped unhurt from the crash. Two crew members were still in intensive care units. All on board the aircraft were believed to be Russians.

The two-year-old Antonov, which is about the size of a Boeing 747, appeared to have aborted the first attempt to land and stalled as it tried to gain altitude to make a fresh approach to the runway, a prefecture official said.
Magistrates said maintenance work had been taking place since August on the landing runway which had been shortened by some 900 metres (yards).
Airport director Carlo Boccardo said the runway was still long enough for a plane the size of an Antonov to land.
Information on the airport work had been communicated to all world airline companies according to air traffic regulations.
Visibility was believed to be fair although it was raining at the time the plane came down.

Boccardo said the airport's ILS and Glidepath systems which allow aircraft to land in limited visibility and indicate the flight path inclination, had been switched off since the maintenance work began.
Such systems were normally deactivated when runway work was being carried out, he said. Airline companies had also been informed of this.
